strengths: Introduces DECO-50, a real-world bimanual dexterous manipulation dataset with tactile sensing and active vision, comprising 4 scenarios, 28 sub-tasks, 50+ hours, ~5M frames, and ~8K successful trajectories, addressing a gap in existing datasets that lack combined bimanual dexterity and tactile data.

Conducts extensive real-world evaluation with over 2,000 robot rollouts across four tasks, including stage-wise and per-object analyses, which provides strong empirical evidence of the method's practical performance.

Proposes a parameter-efficient plugin tactile adapter (LoRA + cross-attention) that improves contact-rich tasks while tuning less than 10% of model parameters, with an ablation showing that decoupled tactile injection (cross-attention) outperforms naive coupled concatenation.

The architecture design is intuitive and well-motivated, using modality-specific conditioning pathways: joint self-attention for vision and action, AdaLN for proprioception and task conditions, and cross-attention for tactile signals, building on successful DiT/MMDiT designs.

Provides an honest discussion of when tactile information is beneficial (contact-rich tasks like waste disposal and assembly) versus when vision and proprioception suffice (pick-and-place, material sorting), and acknowledges limitations such as long-horizon tasks.
weaknesses: Lacks comparison to recent state-of-the-art tactile-aware or VLA policies (e.g., ViTacFormer, Reactive Diffusion Policy, RDT-1B, π0); baselines are limited to ACT and DP, which are relatively old and may not represent the current state of the art.

Experimental confounds are present: DECO uses a ResNet-34 visual encoder while ACT and DP use ResNet-18, and training epochs differ (30 for ACT, 200 for DP, 150 for DECO), potentially giving DECO an unfair advantage and undermining fair comparison.

The claim that the tactile adapter can be incorporated into 'any pretrained vision-based policy' is not demonstrated; it is only applied to DECO, with no experiments on other pretrained policies like DP or ACT.

The ablation comparing coupled vs. decoupled tactile injection (DECO.cs vs. DECO.ds/DECO.p) is limited to two assembly object pairs and does not cover all tasks, weakening the generality of the central claim about decoupled conditioning.
No code or dataset release link is provided despite claiming to release DECO-50, which hinders reproducibility and verification of the dataset contribution.

Models are trained separately per task with a one-hot task condition; no single multi-task or generalist policy is trained, which limits the significance of the dataset for generalist robot learning and reduces the practical impact.

Presentation inconsistencies and errors exist: object naming is inconsistent (e.g., '00081-s12x' vs. '00081-Socket-2x'), Table 4 reports a total of '55/100' instead of '/80', 'Traning Epochs' is misspelled, and citation years are inconsistent (e.g., Zhang et al., 2024 vs. 2025a).

The central claim that 'decoupled multimodal conditioning improves policy performance over coupled fusion' is only partially supported; vision and action tokens are still jointly self-attended, and the observed gains primarily stem from better tactile utilization rather than full decoupling.

No statistical significance tests or confidence intervals are reported; some performance differences (e.g., Task 1: DECO 103/120 vs. ACT 101/120) are within noise, yet the paper claims DECO 'achieves the best performance across all tasks'.
No analysis of inference speed or computational cost is provided, despite claiming DP is slower; only parameter counts are reported, which is insufficient to substantiate the efficiency claims.
Insufficient description of tactile sensor characteristics (sampling rate, calibration, noise) and active camera control, making replication of the hardware setup and data collection difficult.

strengths: A genuine real-robot contribution: a bimanual dexterous manipulation system with tactile sensing evaluated extensively in the real world (over 2,000 rollouts across four tasks with per-object and per-stage breakdowns), which is substantially more evaluation than typical for this class of paper.

The DECO-50 dataset is a useful asset: 50 hours, ~5M frames, 8K successful trajectories, 4 scenarios and 28 sub-tasks, combining bimanual, dexterous hands, tactile sensing, and active binocular vision. Table 9 makes a plausible case that few existing datasets cover all of these simultaneously.

The parameter-efficiency result is meaningful: DECO.p injects tactile with 7.97M trainable parameters (~9.6% of the 83M-parameter backbone) while matching DECO.ds trained from scratch (Table 5), supporting the claim that tactile can be added to a frozen visuomotor policy at low cost.

Sensible conceptual framing: separating weakly tactile-relevant tasks (pick-and-place, material sorting) from strongly tactile-relevant ones (waste disposal, assembly), with stage-wise reporting (Tables 3, 13, 14) that localizes where tactile helps (lid closing, insertion, force monitoring).
The architecture is clearly described and easy to follow, with a clean decoupling of vision (joint self-attention), proprioception (AdaLN), and touch (cross-attention).
weaknesses: The central claim that decoupled conditioning outperforms coupled fusion is not supported by statistically meaningful evidence. DECO vs ACT is 103 vs 101/120 on Pick-and-Place and 101 vs 97/120 on Material Sorting; with ~20 trials per cell and no confidence intervals or significance tests anywhere, these differences are indistinguishable from noise, yet the abstract asserts 'best performance across all tasks' and a '21% improvement over the baseline.'

Baseline comparisons are confounded and therefore unreliable for attributing gains to the architecture: DECO uses ResNet-34 while ACT/DP use ResNet-18; DECO uses flow matching with 5 steps while DP uses DDIM with 10 steps; ACT uses execution chunk size 1 vs 16 for the others; and model sizes differ (51.6M / 76.5M / 83.1M). Any of these could explain the reported gaps.

The ablation actually undercuts the 'decoupled' narrative. DECO.cs (coupled injection) is essentially identical to DECO without tactile at all (33/40 vs 33/40 on stage 1; 28 vs 32 stage 2; 18 vs 21 stage 3), and both DECO.ds and DECO.p use the same cross-attention pathway, so the gains appear to come from cross-attention plus tactile preprocessing rather than from 'decoupling' per se. The paper conflates these two factors and never isolates them.

There is a confound between tactile and warm-starting: DECO.p fine-tunes a pretrained policy whereas DECO.ds is trained from scratch, so the comparison cannot separate the benefit of tactile information from the benefit of starting from a pretrained checkpoint.

No comparison against existing visuo-tactile policies (e.g., ViTacFormer, Reactive Diffusion Policy, TA-VLA, VTLA, ForceVLA) is provided despite these being cited in related work; the only tactile baseline is naive concatenation (DP.t). This makes the claim that the proposed injection mechanism is effective weakly positioned against the literature.

Reproducibility is limited: no code release is mentioned, the dataset release is promised but with no access details, and the tactile encoder (Eq. 4) is described only briefly. The hardware (Unitree H1-2 with Inspire RH56DFTP hands, 17 pads per hand) is specialized, and no sim or cross-embodiment validation is provided.

Presentation and internal-consistency problems reduce confidence in the numbers: Table 1's header reads 'Success Rate 13 / Success Rate 24' with mismatched footnote markers; Table 4 reports DECO.p as '55/100' while all other entries are '/80'; Table 3 (Waste Disposal Stage1 DP.t = 77/80) conflicts with Table 13 (Stage1 DP.t = 77/80 vs the main text's 72/80); and the abstract text appears truncated in the manuscript.

The design principles are asserted rather than demonstrated. There is no ablation isolating individual conditioning pathways (e.g., proprioception via self-attention instead of AdaLN, tactile via AdaLN instead of cross-attention), and no attention/representation analysis showing why decoupling helps, so the 'modalities contribute unequally' hypothesis is not tested.
The generalization claim that the tactile adapter 'can be incorporated into any pretrained vision-based policy' is only demonstrated on DECO itself, so it remains unverified.

strengths: Substantial real-world validation: over 2,000 robot rollouts across four bimanual dexterous tasks (pick-and-place, material sorting, waste disposal, assembly), which is far more extensive than typical manipulation-policy papers and directly supports the empirical claims.

DECO-50 is a genuinely valuable community resource: 50 hours / ~5M frames / ~8K successful trajectories on real dual-arm dexterous hands with tactile sensing and active vision. Table 9 shows it is one of the few datasets combining bimanual, dexterous, tactile, and real data, filling a real gap.

The plugin tactile adapter is a practical and well-motivated contribution: it updates only 7.97M parameters (<10% of the 91.02M model) yet brings ~10.25% average gain and ~20% on contact-rich tasks, demonstrating parameter-efficient injection into a frozen pretrained policy.

The ablation (Table 5) is informative: DECO.cs (coupled injection) performs similarly to vision-only DECO, while DECO.ds (decoupled, from scratch) and DECO.p (adapter) both improve substantially, supporting the claim that how tactile is injected matters more than merely adding it.

Honest and useful task analysis: the paper distinguishes weakly vs strongly tactile-relevant tasks and explicitly concludes that tactile collection may not be justified for pick-and-place/material sorting. This nuanced finding is more valuable than a blanket 'tactile always helps' claim.

Good reproducibility of training setup: Table 10 lists optimizer, betas, weight decay, batch size, LR schedule, epochs, encoders, chunk sizes, samplers, and inference steps; hardware and sensor specifications (Unitree H1-2, Inspire RH56DFTP, 17 pads/hand) are also given.
weaknesses: The central scientific claim—that decoupled conditioning outperforms coupled fusion—is not cleanly isolated. The DECO vs. DP comparison confounds many factors simultaneously: ResNet-34 vs. ResNet-18 encoder, flow-matching vs. DDIM sampler, joint self-attention vs. FiLM conditioning, and 5 vs. 10 inference steps. There is no controlled ablation of the decoupling design on the vision-only policy, so the 'decoupled' framing is over-attributed.

Statistical rigor is limited. Each configuration appears to be a single training run with no error bars, confidence intervals, or seed variance, and evaluation uses only 10–20 trials per object. Several claimed differences (e.g., DECO 72.25% vs. ACT 57.25%) rest on a handful of successes and could be within run-to-run noise.

Headline numbers are under-specified and inconsistently reported. The '21% improvement over the baseline' does not state which baseline, and the abstract's '10.25% average success rate' gain is not tied to a statistical test. Table 4 lists DECO.p's total as 55/100 while all other columns are out of 80 (the appendix Table 14 indicates 55/80), and Table 1's summary rows do not cleanly reconcile with the appendix tables.

Missing comparisons weaken the significance claims. There is no comparison against tactile-aware policies (e.g., ViTacFormer, VTLA, ForceVLA, Reactive Diffusion Policy) or modern VLA baselines (π0, RDT-1B, OpenVLA), so it is unclear whether DECO's gains come from its design or from the dataset and engineering effort.

The material-sorting comparison is confounded by inference latency. The paper itself attributes DP's poor performance to slower inference (10 steps) versus DECO (5 steps) and ACT's temporal ensembling, which means speed—not policy quality—may drive part of the result; this is not controlled for.

Generalization evidence is one-sided: the OOD rows in Table 12 are only reported for DECO variants, with baselines left as '-', so the claim about robustness under distribution shift cannot be compared against alternatives.

The abstract appears truncated in the manuscript (ending at 'Experimental results show that DECO'), and the reference list contains numbering inconsistencies (duplicate indices), which impairs presentation quality.

Reproducibility of the artifacts is incomplete: the dataset is promised but licensing, access, and download details are absent, and no code or checkpoint release is mentioned for the model or adapter.
The limitations discussion is brief and focuses only on long-horizon temporal modeling; it does not acknowledge single-seed evaluation, limited object diversity, or the confounding factors above.

strengths: Significant dataset contribution: DECO-50 provides real-world bimanual dexterous manipulation data with tactile sensing and active vision, comprising 4 scenarios, 28 sub-tasks, ~8K successful trajectories, and ~5M frames (Table 8, Table 11). Such data is scarce and could be a useful community resource.

Extensive real-robot evaluation: over 2,000 rollouts across four tasks, with per-object and stage-wise results and Wilson confidence intervals in the appendix. The gains on contact-rich tasks (Waste Disposal and Assembly) are large and practically meaningful.

Parameter-efficient tactile adaptation: DECO.p updates only 7.97M trainable parameters (<10% of the 91.02M total model) while substantially improving contact-rich task success (Table 6). This supports the claim that tactile can be added to a pretrained visuomotor policy cheaply.

Ablations provide useful evidence for modality-specific injection: DECO.cs vs. DECO.ds/DECO.p (Table 5) shows that naive tactile conditioning is weaker than cross-attention-based decoupled injection, and the permuted-pathway ablation (Table 7) shows that the assignment of proprioception vs. tactile to AdaLN vs. cross-attention matters.

The architecture is clearly motivated and reasonably described: joint self-attention for vision/action tokens, AdaLN for proprioception/task/timestep, and cross-attention for tactile. The two-stage training paradigm is simple and practical.

The paper includes useful implementation details (training epochs, batch size, optimizer, model sizes, tactile encoder design, dataset collection setup) and a ResNet-18 control experiment (Appendix B.3) to partially isolate encoder capacity effects.

Limitations are acknowledged: single hardware platform, normal-force-only tactile sensors, and future work on larger VLAs and cross-embodiment validation. This is appropriate and does not overstate the current scope.
weaknesses: The central claim that decoupled multimodal conditioning improves over coupled fusion is not cleanly isolated. The comparisons to ACT and DP confound architecture (Transformer vs. U-Net), training objective (flow matching vs. DDIM), vision encoder (ResNet-34 vs. ResNet-18), action execution chunk, inference steps, and training epochs. There is no fully coupled multimodal DiT baseline where all modalities are fused equally; the ablations mainly test tactile injection and pathway permutation.

Baselines are limited. The paper compares only ACT, DP, and a naive tactile-concatenation DP.t. It does not compare against recent tactile or visuo-tactile policies discussed in related work (e.g., ViTacFormer, Reactive Diffusion Policy, Tactile-VLA, or adapter-based tactile methods). Therefore, the claim of 'best performance across all tasks' is relative to weak baselines and does not establish state-of-the-art tactile integration.

There is a data-reporting inconsistency between the main text and appendix. Main Table 3 lists DP.t Waste Disposal Stage1=72/80, Stage2=65/80, Stage3=48/80, Results=38/80, while Appendix Table 15 lists DP.t Stage1=77/80, Stage2=43/80, Stage3=38/80. DECO.p Stage2 is 76/80 in the main table but 72/80 in the appendix. Such inconsistencies undermine confidence in the reported numbers.

The policies are trained separately per task with task-level one-hot conditioning rather than as a single multi-task or generalist policy. This weakens the connection to the VLA motivation and limits claims about broad bimanual dexterous manipulation capability.

Evaluation is restricted to a single robot platform, one dexterous hand type, and one tactile sensor modality. Generalization across embodiments, tactile sensors, and larger-scale pretrained VLAs is left as future work, so the practical reach of the adapter is not demonstrated.

Several training and inference choices are not fully controlled: ACT uses execution chunk size 1 with temporal ensembling while DECO uses 16; DP uses 10 DDIM steps while DECO uses 5 flow-matching steps; training epochs differ substantially. These choices may affect success rates and make the baseline comparison less conclusive.

Main-table results do not report uncertainty or statistical tests, and many per-task gains are within overlapping Wilson intervals. The aggregate gains are plausible, but the evidence for improvements on weakly tactile-relevant tasks is weaker than the headline numbers suggest.

Reproducibility is only partially supported. The PDF text mentions code, project page, and dataset links but the actual URLs are not visible in the manuscript. Key details such as train/validation splits, checkpoint selection protocol, cross-attention head configuration, and exact LoRA application points are missing or ambiguous. The tactile encoder description in Appendix B.1 is difficult to parse precisely.

The contribution of the active camera is not ablated. Since active-camera joints are part of the state/action space, it is unclear how much of the visual improvement comes from active vision versus the proposed decoupled architecture.

Dataset scale is modest compared with large-scale robot datasets (e.g., RoboMIND 2.0 with 1000+ hours), although the tactile bimanual dexterous modality makes it relatively unique. Generalization and long-horizon robustness are not extensively evaluated.

strengths: Targets a genuinely hard and underexplored setting: real-world bimanual dexterous manipulation with tactile sensing, evaluated on real hardware with a large number of rollouts (2000+), which is rare and valuable.

The DECO-50 dataset (50 hours, ~5M frames, ~8K successful trajectories, 4 scenarios / 28 sub-tasks, tactile + active binocular vision) is a substantial and lasting resource that fills a real gap noted in Table 11 (few datasets combine bimanual, dexterous, tactile, and real).

The plugin tactile adapter is a practical contribution: Table 6 shows only 7.97M trainable parameters (vs. ~83-89M for from-scratch variants) while achieving performance comparable to the from-scratch decoupled model (DECO.ds), demonstrating parameter-efficient tactile injection into a frozen pretrained policy.

The evaluation is unusually detailed and transparent: per-task, per-object, and per-stage breakdowns with Wilson 95% confidence intervals (Tables 13-16), plus a control experiment swapping ResNet-34 for ResNet-18 (Tables 17-20) to isolate encoder capacity from the conditioning design.

The pathway-assignment ablation (Table 7) and coupled-vs-decoupled tactile ablation (Table 5) provide some direct evidence for the central design hypothesis, with the coupled variant (DECO.cs) failing to match the decoupled variants.
weaknesses: The core methodological novelty is incremental. The 'decoupled' design is essentially a recombination of standard DiT conditioning mechanisms: joint self-attention between vision and action tokens, AdaLN for global conditions (proprioception/timestep/task), and cross-attention for auxiliary signals. This closely mirrors prior work (e.g., MMDiT, pi_0-style AdaLN conditioning), so the 'decoupled paradigm' framing overstates the conceptual advance.

Baselines are weak and outdated for the claim being made. Only ACT and DP (plus a naive concatenation variant DP.t) are compared, despite the related work explicitly discussing more relevant tactile-aware policies (Higuera et al.'s tactile adapter, ViTacFormer, Reactive Diffusion Policy, Tactile-VLA, OmniVTLA). Without any modern tactile-fusion or VLA baseline, the central claim that DECO's injection scheme is superior is not convincingly established.

Headline claims are vague and under-specified. The abstract/Table 1 report 'a 21% improvement over the baseline' without naming the baseline (DP at 51.25% gives 21.0%, ACT at 57.25% gives 15.0%), and the definition of 'contact-rich' aggregate rates (footnotes 1/3 vs 2/4) is confounded by the mangled table headers.

The decoupling evidence is narrower than the claim. Table 5 shows the coupled tactile variant (DECO.cs) behaves only marginally differently from DECO without tactile, and the cleanest test of decoupling (Table 7) is a somewhat artificial strawman: injecting 28 proprioceptive joints as a cross-attention sequence is an unnatural configuration, so the dramatic drop (0/40 on Stage 3) may reflect that mismatch rather than validating 'modality-to-pathway assignment' in general.

Statistical rigor is limited. Several per-object gains (e.g., Table 2/Table 5 individual cells) fall within overlapping Wilson intervals, and there is no formal significance testing; with 10-20 trials per cell, small differences are not reliably interpretable.

Presentation and reproducibility details need work: truncated abstract text, malformed Table 1 headers ('Success Rate 13', 'Success Rate 24'), a confusing tactile-encoder equation (Eq. 4) that does not clearly match the described average-pooling + linear-projection + gating pipeline, and redundant figures (Figs. 1/3/4).

External validity is limited to a single hardware platform and one tactile sensor (Inspire RH56DFTP, normal-force-only piezoresistive pads). This is acknowledged, but it bounds the generality of the tactile-adapter claims and of the 'decoupling matters' conclusion.

strengths: Substantial real-world empirical contribution: bimanual dexterous manipulation with tactile sensing evaluated over four tasks / 28 sub-tasks with 2,000+ real robot rollouts, and reported with Wilson 95% confidence intervals (Tables 13-16).

DECO-50 is a genuinely useful resource: a bimanual, dexterous-hand, tactile, real-world dataset (50h, ~5M frames, ~8K successful trajectories), and Table 11 positions it clearly against existing datasets where bimanual+dexterous+tactile+real is scarce.

The plugin tactile adapter is convincingly parameter-efficient: only 7.97M trainable parameters (tactile encoder, cross-attention K/V, LoRA rank 32) reach performance comparable to DECO.ds trained from scratch (Tables 5-6), which is a practically meaningful result for adapting pretrained policies.

The conditioning-pathway permutation ablation (Table 7) is a strong and informative experiment: swapping proprioception to cross-attention and tactile to AdaLN collapses Stage 3 from 29/40 to 0/40, giving concrete evidence that modality-to-pathway assignment matters rather than merely asserting it.
The ResNet-18 vs ResNet-34 control (Tables 17-20) reasonably isolates encoder capacity from the architectural claim, showing DECO(ResNet-18) still outperforms the baselines.

The paper makes a useful conceptual distinction between weakly tactile-relevant (pick-and-place, material sorting) and strongly tactile-relevant (waste disposal, assembly) tasks, and its per-stage analysis (Tables 3, 15, 16) supports the claim that tactile primarily helps contact-rich subgoals.
Limitations are honestly discussed (single hardware platform, one hand/tactile sensor type, no temporal/memory modeling), and the ethics/impact statement is appropriately minimal.
weaknesses: Baselines are weak relative to the paper's own framing. The introduction situates DECO among VLAs (RT-1, RDT-1B, OpenVLA, pi0), yet the only comparisons are ACT and Diffusion Policy, with DP.t as the sole tactile baseline. The headline "best performance across all tasks" is therefore established only against relatively simple visuomotor baselines, and no VLA/tactile-VLA baselines (e.g., ViTacFormer, Tactile-VLA) are compared.

The central "decoupling beats coupling" claim is not cleanly isolated for the vision pathway. DECO vs DP contrasts entire architectures (joint self-attention for vision+action vs FiLM conditioning), so the gain cannot be attributed to decoupling per se; no ablation holds the backbone fixed while varying only the visual/proprioceptive injection mechanism.

Reproducibility is currently not verifiable: the Code / Project Page / Dataset links are placeholders, and the Appendix B.1 sentence "All hyperparameters and training configurations are provided in the open-sourced code at" is truncated. No actual artifacts are available in the manuscript as presented.

No statistical significance testing between methods. Several reported gaps fall within overlapping Wilson intervals (e.g., DECO 103/120 vs DECO.p 108/120 on Task 1; DECO vs DECO.p on Task 2), and the claim of a "21% improvement" is relative to the specific DP baseline and ambiguously phrased.

Presentation defects reduce confidence: Table 1 headers are mangled ("Success Rate 13", "Success Rate 24"), Table 16 loses its confidence-interval bracket formatting, and the Figure 6 caption references (a)-(f) that are not clearly matched to the described items (e.g., "piece-correspondence mapping").

Ablations of the tactile module itself are thin: the tactile encoder gating (Eq. 4), the choice of cross-attention vs alternatives, and the LoRA rank are not ablated, so the design of the adapter is asserted rather than systematically validated. The sensor measures only normal force (no shear), which is acknowledged but limits the scope of the tactile claims.

Evaluation is confined to one hardware platform with custom tasks and object sets, so generalization of both the architecture and the adapter beyond this setup is untested (acknowledged, but it materially limits the reach of the claims).

strengths: Extensive real-world evaluation with over 2,000 rollouts across four tasks and 28 sub-tasks, including stage-wise success statistics and Wilson confidence intervals, provides unusually strong empirical evidence for a manipulation policy paper.

The plugin tactile adapter is genuinely parameter-efficient (7.97M trainable parameters, <10% of the model) and is shown to match the performance of training a tactile-aware policy from scratch (DECO.p vs DECO.ds in Table 5), demonstrating a practical path to adding touch to pretrained visuomotor policies.

DECO-50 is a useful community resource: a real-world bimanual dexterous manipulation dataset with tactile sensing and active vision (50 hours, ~5M frames, 8K successful trajectories), filling a gap noted in the dataset comparison (Table 11).

The ablations are informative, particularly the modality-to-pathway permutation study (Table 7), which shows a dramatic drop (Stage 3: 0/40 vs 29/40) when proprioception is routed through cross-attention and tactile through AdaLN, supporting the design choice.

The paper is honest about when tactile helps: it explicitly reports that pick-and-place and material sorting are weakly tactile-relevant and that tactile collection may not be justified there, and it transparently reports the null tactile result on UniVTAC.
Reproducibility is addressed with detailed hyperparameters (Tables 12), code/dataset/weights released, and supplementary simulation evaluations on LIBERO, RoboTwin 2.0, UniVTAC, and DexJoCo.
weaknesses: The central claim that decoupled conditioning drives performance gains is not cleanly isolated in the main experiments: DECO is compared mainly against ACT and DP, which differ in architecture, sampler (DDIM vs flow matching), inference steps, execution chunk size, and encoder, confounding the comparison. The decoupling benefit is only demonstrated in a limited ablation on two assembly object pairs.

The tactile adapter yields no gain in simulation on UniVTAC (Table 23: DECO 82.1% vs DECO.p 82.1%), with failure modes unchanged; while honestly reported, this undercuts the generality of the claim that the adapter effectively exploits touch for contact-rich tasks.

Statistical treatment is weak: many key comparisons have overlapping Wilson 95% confidence intervals (e.g., Task 1 DECO 103/120 vs DECO.p 108/120; Task 2 DECO 101/120 vs DECO.p 105/120; Waste Disposal Stage 1 DECO 71/80 vs DECO.p 76/80), yet no significance testing is performed, and the headline '21% improvement over the baseline' does not specify which baseline, making the magnitude of the contribution hard to assess.

The specific modality-to-pathway assignment (proprioception/timestep/task via AdaLN; tactile via cross-attention) is largely asserted rather than derived, and the supporting evidence is a single permutation ablation on two object pairs; it is unclear how robust this assignment is across tasks and sensors.

Presentation problems reduce clarity: the Table 1 header appears garbled ('Success Rate 13', 'Success Rate 24'), reference formatting is inconsistent, and there are figure/caption mismatches (e.g., Figure 7 caption references waste disposal and assembly while the text discusses interference-fit stages).

The dataset, while unique in combining bimanual dexterity, tactile, and real-world data, is comparatively small in hours (50 vs 305-1000+ for several datasets in Table 11), and there is no cross-embodiment or cross-dataset generalization study despite this being listed as future work.

strengths: Tackles a genuinely hard and valuable problem: real-world bimanual dexterous manipulation with tactile sensing, evaluated with a substantial number of real robot rollouts (>2,000), which is rare and costly.

Releases DECO-50, a bimanual dexterous manipulation dataset with tactile sensing and active binocular vision (~50 hours, ~5M frames, ~8K successful trajectories), which is a useful community resource and is well documented in the appendix (sensor layout, collection protocol, comparison table).

The plugin tactile adapter is practically appealing: it injects tactile into a frozen pretrained policy via cross-attention + LoRA while updating only 7.97M parameters (Table 6), and DECO.p is reported as comparable to the from-scratch decoupled variant (DECO.ds).

The pathway-assignment ablation (Table 7) is a clean, well-motivated controlled experiment showing that swapping proprioception and tactile injection pathways collapses Stage 3 performance (29/40 to 0/40), giving concrete evidence that modality-to-pathway assignment matters.
The paper reports a null/negative result honestly (tactile adapter gives no average gain on UniVTAC, Table 23) and includes a limitation discussion rather than overclaiming, which is good practice.

Simulation results across four benchmarks (LIBERO, RoboTwin 2.0, UniVTAC, DexJoCo) suggest the policy is not narrowly overfit to the authors' platform, and the appendix provides extensive per-object/per-stage breakdowns with Wilson intervals.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty. The core block is essentially standard MMDiT/DiT: joint self-attention between image and action tokens plus AdaLN conditioning on proprioception/timestep/task (Eq. 3). The added ingredients (LoRA, cross-attention for tactile) are existing techniques. The paper does not clearly delineate what is genuinely new versus a recombination of Peebles & Xie (2023), Hu et al. (2021), and standard cross-attention.

The central claim (decoupled injection improves over coupled fusion) is not cleanly tested. The main comparison is against ACT and DP, which differ in architecture, training schedule, and encoder, so improvements cannot be attributed to decoupling. There is no coupled-MMDiT baseline for the vision/proprioception pathways, which is the exact contrast the framing requires.

The key supporting ablation is weak/mixed. In Table 5, coupled tactile (DECO.cs) is essentially indistinguishable from vision-only DECO (33/33/21 vs 33/28/18 totals), so the 'coupling is insufficient' conclusion rests on a single comparison, and the decoupled-vs-coupled distinction is only demonstrated for tactile, not for the broader paradigm.

The tactile adapter's general value is undercut by simulation: on UniVTAC it yields no average improvement (82.1% vs 82.1%) and actually degrades insert_hole (59 vs 63); the failure breakdown shows only marginal slip reduction (e.g., 37 to 41 on insert_hole). This materially weakens the claim that the plugin adapter is broadly effective.

Statistical significance is not established for several headline comparisons. Many Wilson intervals overlap (e.g., Task 1 DECO 103/120 vs DECO.p 108/120; Task 2 DECO 101/120 vs DECO.p 105/120), yet strong claims such as '21% improvement over the baseline' and '10.25% additional success' are presented as definitive without significance testing or multiple-comparison control.

Potential baseline unfairness. Training epochs differ sharply (ACT 30, DP 200, DECO 150, Table 12), ACT uses execution chunk size 1 with a temporal ensembler while others use 16, and DP's U-Net channels were manually reduced; these choices could bias the comparison and are not justified or ablated.

Reproducibility is limited by presentation: the code, project page, and dataset links are blank in the manuscript, and the paper relies on external assets (AutoMate object IDs, custom prints) that are only partially specified. The two strongest novelty-adjacent claims (decoupling, pathway assignment) are each supported by a single experiment of 40 trials on two object pairs, which is a thin basis for a strong causal conclusion.

Presentation problems reduce clarity: garbled table headers ('Success Rate 13', 'Success Rate 24' in Table 1), inconsistent naming of variants (DECO.cs/DECO.ds/DECO.p, DP.t) across text and tables, and figure/caption misalignment (e.g., Figure 7 referenced without a clear self-contained caption).

strengths: Real-world bimanual dexterous manipulation with tactile sensing is convincingly evaluated: 4 tasks, 28 sub-tasks, over 2,000 robot rollouts, with consistent gains over ACT and DP baselines. The release of DECO-50 (50 hours, ~5M frames, ~8K successful trajectories, with active vision and tactile) is a substantial and valuable community resource.

The plugin tactile adapter is genuinely parameter-efficient: only 7.97M trainable parameters (tactile encoder, cross-attention, LoRA) versus 83M for the full policy, yet achieves performance comparable to the from-scratch decoupled variant (DECO.ds) and improves over vision-only DECO, especially on contact-rich tasks (e.g., +20% average success on Waste Disposal and Assembly).

The pathway-assignment ablation (Table 7) is a particularly strong piece of evidence: swapping proprioception into cross-attention and tactile into AdaLN collapses Stage 3 performance from 29/40 to 0/40, supporting the central claim that the specific modality-to-pathway assignment matters.

The analysis of which tasks benefit from tactile is systematic and honest: weakly tactile-relevant tasks (Pick and Place, Material Sorting) see little gain, while strongly contact-rich tasks (Waste Disposal, Assembly) benefit substantially, matching the stated hypothesis and failure analysis.

Reproducibility is well addressed: code, dataset, and trained weights for simulation benchmarks are promised/released; detailed hyperparameters (Table 12) and training setup are provided; the ResNet-18 ablation cleanly isolates encoder capacity from the decoupled conditioning design.

Supplementary simulation results on LIBERO, RoboTwin 2.0, UniVTAC, and DexJoCo show competitive performance with a small (~80M) model and no external pretraining, suggesting the architecture generalizes beyond the custom real-world setup.
The limitations discussion is honest, acknowledging single-platform evaluation and lack of temporal modeling.
weaknesses: The architectural novelty is incremental: the model combines standard MMDiT components (joint self-attention for vision/action, AdaLN for proprioception/timestep/task) with a LoRA + cross-attention tactile adapter. The 'decoupled' idea is intuitive but not deeply novel, and the paper provides limited theoretical insight into why this specific decoupling should be optimal.

The central claim that decoupled conditioning improves over coupled fusion is supported mainly by one coupled variant (DECO.cs) and the pathway permutation ablation. DECO.cs still outperforms vision-only DECO on several sub-tasks (e.g., IF Stage 1: 15/20 vs. 13/20; IF Stage 2: 15/20 vs. 11/20), so the evidence that coupling is harmful is not uniformly strong, and other coupling mechanisms are not explored.

The main real-world comparison lacks formal statistical significance testing. Wilson confidence intervals are reported in the appendix, and while some differences are clearly significant, the headline '21% improvement' is relative to DP (51.25%) rather than to the strongest baseline ACT (57.25%), making the absolute improvement over the best baseline ~15%.

The tactile adapter shows essentially no benefit in the UniVTAC simulation benchmark (DECO 82.1 vs. DECO.p 82.1) and only marginal slip reduction, which weakens the generality of the tactile-adaptation claim across domains. The authors acknowledge this but it remains a limitation for the 'tactile can be effectively added to pretrained policies' narrative.

The tactile sensors measure only normal force (no shear/tangential components), which restricts the richness of contact information available to the adapter and may limit the scope of tasks that can benefit.

Minor presentation issues: typos in tables ('Success Rate 13' in Table 1, 'Traning Epochs' in Table 12), and the code/dataset links are placeholders in the submitted version, slightly reducing immediate reproducibility.
